h6: Cross-Cloud Disaster Recovery for SAP HANA: Building Resilience Beyond a Single Cloud
p: Cross-Cloud Disaster Recovery for SAP HANA: Building Resilience Beyond a Single Cloud

Most enterprises run their critical SAP HANA workloads such as finance, supply chain, and order management on a single cloud provider. While convenient, this creates a significant risk: a regional outage or cloud provider disruption can impact the entire SAP landscape. Cross-Cloud Disaster Recovery (DR) addresses this challenge by hosting the production SAP HANA environment on one cloud platform (such as AWS) while maintaining a synchronized disaster recovery environment on another cloud provider (such as Google Cloud).

For most enterprises running SAP HANA, the database sits at the heart of every critical business process order management, finance, supply chain and more, yet many organizations still run their entire SAP landscape inside a single public cloud region, which means a single regional outage, platform incident or provider-level disruption can bring core operations to a halt. As reliance on cloud infrastructure grows, so does the need for a resilient, provider-independent disaster recovery (DR) strategy that doesn’t leave business continuity hostage to one vendor’s availability zone.

This is where Cross-Cloud Disaster Recovery comes in an architecture that keeps your SAP HANA production database on one cloud (e.g., AWS) while maintaining a fully synchronized, ready-to-activate secondary environment on another (Google Cloud). Below, we break down why this approach matters, how it works end-to-end and the trade-offs to weigh before adopting it.

A cross-cloud DR architecture for SAP HANA keeps your production environment running on your primary cloud provider while replicating data in near real-time to a completely separate cloud provider acting as the disaster recovery site. Instead of relying on a single vendor’s infrastructure end-to-end, this model introduces true provider diversity so a regional outage, platform-level incident, or even a full provider disruption on the primary side doesn’t take your SAP operations down with it.

Cross-Cloud Disaster Recovery, the primary cloud (e.g., AWS Mumbai) continues running production, while Google Cloud serves as the dedicated DR site for SAP HANA, delivering cloud-provider independence and infrastructure redundancy.

Near Real-Time Replication, SAP HANA System Replication (HSR) continuously syncs transactional data across both clouds, achieving a low Recovery Point Objective (RPO) with minimal data loss during failover.
Business Continuity, DR best practices, controlled failover procedures and recovery runbooks ensure rapid restoration of SAP services and continuity of mission-critical processes.
Enterprise-Grade Availability, a modern architecture spanning HANA replication, cross-cloud connectivity, DR orchestration, RPO/RTO objectives and operational governance.
Provider independence, removes single-vendor concentration risk by spreading production and DR across two different cloud providers.
Geographic separation, a distant secondary region isolates the DR environment from regional or platform-wide outages affecting the primary cloud.
Elastic DR capacity, scale recovery resources on demand and pay only for what you use, rather than maintaining a fully-provisioned standby at all times.
Low RPO, fast RTO — continuous SAP HANA System Replication can achieve near-zero data loss (RPO as low as 30 minutes) and orchestrated failover that restores SAP services within 60–120 minutes.
Global network & security, low-latency replication with enterprise-grade compliance across cloud boundaries.
Cross-cloud network egress — replication traffic between providers incurs additional data transfer costs that must be factored into the overall TCO.
Operational complexity — maintaining two different cloud environments in sync (kernel updates, profiles, transport directories, certificates) requires disciplined change management.
Manual synchronization overhead — SAP Application Server configuration on the DR side is typically maintained manually unless automation is explicitly built into the design.
DNS and external traffic redirection — unless automated, failover requires manual DNS cutover, which adds a coordination step during an actual disaster.

The proposed solution introduces robust, scalable cross-cloud DR architecture designed specifically for SAP workloads, the primary cloud environment continues operating as the production site, hosting the SAP HANA primary database and SAP application servers, data replication is accomplished using SAP HANA System Replication (HSR) operating in asynchronous mode, ensuring near real-time synchronization between production and disaster recovery environments, secure connectivity between the two cloud providers is established through a highly available VPN or dedicated cross-cloud interconnect, supporting reliable data movement across cloud boundaries, on the disaster recovery side, the secondary cloud region hosts the SAP HANA secondary system together with standby SAP application servers, ready for activation during a recovery event.
Normal Operation Flow — users access SAP services via DNS, directing traffic to the primary cloud’s SAP application servers connected to the primary HANA database.
Database Replication — SAP HANA System Replication continuously syncs database changes from the primary environment to the secondary cloud environment.
Failover Activation — on disaster detection, the secondary cloud’s HANA database is promoted to primary status, and SAP applications are activated for failover.
Validation & User Redirection — validation confirms application and database integrity; DNS updates then redirect users to the secondary cloud environment with minimal interruption.
One of the more nuanced decisions in designing a cross-cloud DR strategy is whether failover should be manual or automated  and each comes with distinct trade-offs.
Business approval ensures failover only happens for genuine disaster events, not false alarms.
The SAP team validates HANA replication, services, and application health before recovery begins.
DNS cutover only happens after successful SAP validation, reducing the risk of premature disruption.
Lower implementation complexity, with easier troubleshooting and full customer control over failover and failback timing.
Recovery is faster since it follows predefined logic without waiting for manual sign-off.
Carries a risk of failover being triggered by false alarms, monitoring glitches, or temporary outages.
Scripts validate infrastructure readiness but not business transaction integrity or application-level readiness.
Requires greater upfront investment in script development, testing, and governance — best suited for organizations with mature DR orchestration maturity.

This blog is written for technology and business leaders who are responsible for the resilience, uptime and continuity of mission-critical SAP HANA environments — particularly those who are still dependent on a single cloud provider and are beginning to question what happens when that provider has a bad day.
CIOs, CTOs and IT Directors - evaluating enterprise risk exposure from single-cloud concentration and looking for a strategic, board-level answer to “what’s our SAP DR posture?”
Cloud and Enterprise Architects - designing multi-cloud or provider-independent infrastructure strategies and needing a reference architecture for cross-cloud replication, connectivity and failover.

SAP Basis and SAP HANA Administrators - responsible for configuring, monitoring and maintaining HANA System Replication (HSR), and who need to understand the operational realities of running HSR across cloud boundaries.
Disaster Recovery (DR) and Business Continuity (BCP) Planners - defining RPO/RTO targets, recovery runbooks and failover governance for critical ERP workloads.

Infrastructure and Cloud Operations Teams - managing day-to-day cross-cloud connectivity, network egress costs, certificate/profile synchronization and change management across two provider environments.

Enterprises running SAP on AWS, Azure or GCP as a single-cloud deployment - who are exploring whether a secondary cloud DR site is a practical, cost-elastic alternative to a second on-prem or same-provider DR region.

Cross-cloud disaster recovery for SAP HANA is no longer a nice-to-have  for organizations running mission-critical ERP workloads on a single cloud provider, it’s a strategic necessity. By pairing SAP HANA System Replication with a secondary cloud environment, enterprises gain provider independence, geographic isolation from regional outages, and a clear path to low RPO and fast RTO recovery, all while keeping costs elastic rather than fixed. The right balance between manual, business-approved failover and automated recovery ultimately depends on your organization’s operational maturity and risk appetite, regardless of which path you choose, a well-architected cross-cloud DR strategy ensures that a single point of failure never becomes a single point of business disruption.

h6: The Autonomous Engineering Era
p: A deep dive into Google Antigravity via Gemini Enterprise, covering agent orchestration, enterprise use cases, verification, security, deployment, and Quadra Systems’ services.

Imagine an engineer assigned a critical bug report at 4:30 PM. Instead of manually digging through legacy code, writing patches, running builds, and testing viewports, an AI agent takes the ticket, fixes the backend bug, executes the test suite, captures video proof in a browser, and submits a green pull request for approval.
This is not a future concept—it is the reality of the Autonomous Engineering Era. We are witnessing a fundamental shift: moving from AI that reacts to AI that acts.

Google Antigravity transforms software delivery by advancing beyond simple inline code completion and basic chat prompts. Powered by Latest Gemini Flash Models—delivering up to 12x faster execution speeds and benchmark-leading performance on complex tasks—Antigravity’s agents plan complex tasks, write code, execute builds and test suites in the terminal, and visually verify UI outcomes in a browser—handing back fully validated, auditable results to your engineering team.
That capability introduces critical architectural and operational choices for enterprise leadership: Where does the agent run, how is it contained, and how is it licensed?

Google Antigravity is built to be Enterprise Ready, featuring built-in security guardrails, workspace sandboxing, lifecycle policy hooks, and full integration with your existing Google Cloud environment. Access is flexible across select Gemini Enterprise app subscriptions and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform API with consumption-based pricing.
In this deep dive, we examine Antigravity’s core capabilities, real-world high-ROI use cases, architectural advantages, and the security controls that make agentic automation adoptable at scale.

Google Antigravity expands into a complete ecosystem powered by a shared agent harness co-trained with Gemini models. Within a single task, the platform operates seamlessly across four primary surfaces:
A standalone application that acts as a central hub for agent interaction and multi-agent management.
A high-velocity command-line surface designed for terminal-first developers and scripting.
Programmatic access to the Antigravity agent harness, enabling custom agent behaviors hosted on your infrastructure of choice.
Integrates directly into IDEs for code editing, architecture planning, and file updates.
Across these surfaces, agents coordinate across three operational loops:
Editor: Plans, structures, and writes multi-file code changes.
Terminal: Executes build scripts, linting, and automated test suites via Gemini 3.5 Flash.
Browser: Drives live UI testing via a subagent integrated with Chrome DevTools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), generating screen recordings and visual proof.

The primary agent programmatically spawns subagents in specialized, cloned, or dynamically defined roles. Subagents inherit only the parent’s explicitly configured tools and permissions—delegation is strictly non-escalating. For complex initiatives, Agent Teams can be orchestrated asynchronously across isolated Git worktrees, allowing parallel execution without branch conflicts or dirty workspace states.

Software engineering teams lose hundreds of hours onboarding developers to legacy systems or complex microservice architectures. Stale README files and undocumented extension patterns force senior architects to spend hours delivering repetitive walkthroughs.
An engineer points Antigravity to a local or remote repository.
The agent analyzes the live directory structure, dependency graph, and implementation patterns.
It generates an interactive Implementation Plan and Walkthrough detailing data flow, architectural boundaries, and step-by-step guidance on where to inject new features.
75% reduction in developer onboarding time, turning days of manual architecture reviews into a 10-minute automated overview.
A critical checkout error breaks during peak promotion hours. Reproducing, fixing, and verifying the bug across multiple mobile viewports consumes hours of engineering capacity.
The agent reproduces the bug in a headless browser using Chrome DevTools via MCP.
It traces the failure to a currency rounding bug in the pricing service, applies the patch, and runs the local test suite.
It re-executes the checkout flow, capturing a video recording and screenshots as visual evidence of resolution.
80% drop in Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR)—slashing bug resolution from 4 hours to under 20 minutes while providing visual proof to QA and CAB stakeholders.
Upgrading a mandatory security dependency across 12 microservices requires 12 separate repository setups, manual context switching, running 12 test suites, and opening 12 pull requests.
A coordinating agent spawns 12 parallel subagents in isolated Git worktrees.
Each subagent applies the patch, runs local tests, and opens a pull request.
Subagents flag breaking API changes for human review while cleanly submitting green-build pull requests ready for approval.
90% reduction in developer labor hours, turning a week-long maintenance chore into a 30-minute background job.

Cron-style triggers launch agents autonomously against defined prompts and repositories without human invocation—converting recurring engineering maintenance into reliable background jobs. In addition, JSON Lifecycle Hooks allow security teams to enforce policy-as-code at critical execution milestones (e.g., pre-command execution, post-file modification, or pre-PR creation):
Pull Request Pre-Review: Analyzes open PRs against internal coding standards, flagging missing test coverage or unhandled exceptions before human review.
Nightly Vulnerability Sweeps: Scans dependency manifests for active CVE advisories, submitting contextual code patches rather than raw alert dumps.
Secret & Credential Scans: Continuously scans source code and configuration files for exposed API keys, credentials, and connection strings via pre-commit lifecycle hooks.
Dependency Hygiene & Modern Web Guidance: Upgrades minor dependencies weekly, validates against web best practices, and submits ready-to-test change sets.
Documentation Sync: Reconciles API implementations against developer documentation, flagging out-of-date sections.
Every agent run produces structured deliverables designed to fit seamlessly into corporate Change Advisory Board (CAB) and compliance processes:
Steerable, human-reviewable roadmap generated before file modifications.
Eliminates rogue code changes and misaligned requirements.
Standard Git line-level changes with explicit approval gates.
Preserves standard code-review and PR workflows.
Narrative summary detailing what changed and why.
Accelerates documentation and team knowledge sharing.
Screen recordings and screenshots of end-to-end UI verification.
Provides verifiable proof for audit, QA, and regulatory compliance.
Conventional developer tools operate in narrow silos:
Isolated AI Editors: Possess file context but lack execution and verification capabilities.
Chat-Based CLI Wrappers: Have terminal access but generate unstructured transcripts rather than auditable artefacts.
Inline Completion Assistants: Optimize for keystroke latency, addressing a fundamentally different autocomplete task.
Antigravity stands apart across three core architectural pillars:

Why This Guide Exists

h6: From Legacy VMs to Cloud-Native Applications: Practical Workload Migration Strategies with Google Kubernetes Engine.
p: From Legacy VMs to Cloud-Native Applications: Practical Workload Migration Strategies with Google Kubernetes Engine.

Many VM-to-GKE migrations appear successful at cutover, but issues surface later: OOMKilled events, HTTP 502 responses during rollout, or data loss from local container storage. Early workload assessment prevents most of these failures.
Kubernetes exposes assumptions that long-lived virtual machines can hide, especially around memory, storage, identity, startup, and shutdown.
The guide follows the migration lifecycle from assessment to decommissioning and focuses on decisions with lasting operational impact.
This guide turns recurring migration lessons into a practical review path for engineers modernising applications on Google Cloud.
·       Building a container image that behaves correctly under an orchestrator
·       Creating a GKE cluster with the security and networking defaults set correctly the first time
·       Writing a Deployment that survives rescheduling, rollouts and node upgrades
·       Cutting over as a weighted traffic shift, with a rollback that actually works
·       The seven failure modes behind most post-migration incidents
•         Assess each workload separately. Replatform, refactor, rehost, or defer based on evidence.
•         Measure CPU, memory, ports, storage writes, dependencies, and latency before defining container resources.
•         Use Workload Identity Federation instead of exported service account keys.
•         Plan VPC-native networking and IP ranges before cluster creation.
•         Use startup, readiness, and liveness probes for different health decisions.
•         Move production traffic in controlled stages and retain a tested rollback path.
•         Decommission the legacy environment only after validation, ownership approval, and retention checks.
Twelve terms that the rest of this guide uses without stopping to explain. If these are already familiar, skip ahead.
The whole GKE environment: a control plane plus the machines that run your applications
The Google-managed brain of the cluster. It decides what runs where. You never patch or restart it
One virtual machine inside the cluster. Your application actually runs here
The smallest thing GKE runs: one or more containers that share an IP address and start and stop together. Pods are disposable and get replaced routinely
A packaged, read-only snapshot of your application and everything it needs to run
Where container images are stored so the cluster can download them
The object that says “keep three copies of this pod running”. It recreates pods when they die and handles version upgrades
One running copy of the pod. Three replicas means three copies
A YAML file describing what you want to exist. You send it to the cluster and the cluster reconciles reality against it
Replacing running pods with a new version, a few at a time, without taking the service down
A health check GKE runs against your container to decide whether it is alive and whether it should receive traffic
A folder inside the cluster that keeps one team's workloads separate from another's
Two platform changes affect migration planning and older implementation guidance.

Container Registry as a Google-hosted product is gone. Writes to gcr.io stopped on 18 March 2025, reads stopped on 3 June 2025, and from 14 October 2025 all gcr.io URLs are served from Artifact Registry, with anything never copied across now unavailable.

Any tutorial that tells you to configure Docker authentication with no arguments and push to a gcr.io path is describing a service that no longer accepts your images. Artifact Registry is the target, and its hostnames are regional — the location is baked into the hostname rather than passed as a setting. A repository in Mumbai lives under an asia-south1 host, and an image reference that omits the region will not resolve.

A Compute Class is a workload-level setting that tells GKE what kind of node to run a pod on. Autopilot ComputeClasses are now available inside Standard clusters, which means you can run specific workloads in Autopilot mode — Google-managed nodes, billed per pod request — while the rest of the cluster stays on node pools you control.
This allows a Standard cluster to retain self-managed node pools while selected, validated workloads use an Autopilot ComputeClass.
Strategy is set per workload, not per estate. Most teams replatform first — container in, architecture unchanged — and refactor later, against real production telemetry rather than assumptions.
Container the application with minimal change; architecture stays as it is
The app containerizes cleanly, or you are exiting a data centre on a deadline
Decompose into services, externalize state, adopt cloud-native patterns
The workload is strategically important and release velocity is the constraint
Lift to a VM, or leave where it is
Rare batch jobs, vendor appliances, anything needing kernel modules or host access
Not every workload belongs on GKE. Infrequent jobs, appliances, or host-dependent applications may be better rehosted or deferred.
Work through these before the first workload moves. Each has an artifact that proves it is done — a written answer, a diagram, a captured baseline. “We discussed it” does not count.
Every workload has a written answer to: where does it write? Anything writing to local disk needs a PersistentVolume or externalization before it moves
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)-native cluster, with pod and service IP ranges sized for three years of growth. Range exhaustion cannot be fixed in place
Workload Identity enabled, so pods authenticate as a Google service account without a key file. No exported service account keys anywhere in the design
Databases and file shares have their own track (Database Migration Service, Storage Transfer Service) with a tested rollback
Current 50th, 95th and 99th percentile (p50, p95, p99) latency, error rate and resource use captured from the legacy system
An observability baseline provides the evidence needed to confirm that latency, errors, and resource behaviour have not regressed after cutover.

A workload on a virtual machine with 4 virtual CPUs (vCPU) and 16 GB of memory almost certainly does not need 4 vCPU and 16 GB. That figure was chosen years ago with a comfortable margin, and copying it into a resource request carries the guess forward and multiplies it by the replica count.
Instead, capture what the application actually uses over a full business cycle, month-end included. Three measurements are worth taking before anything moves:
•     Peak memory and CPU across a sampling window long enough to include the busiest hour of the busiest day, not an average over a quiet afternoon.
•     Every port the process is listening on. Each one becomes a Service definition, and any port nobody can account for is a finding in itself.

•     Open file handles against the local filesystem, excluding shared libraries. This is the list that tells you which workloads are quietly stateful — and it is almost always longer than the team expects.

Workload Identity, Secret Manager, centralised logging and the VPC design are far cheaper to get right before the first workload moves than to retrofit across forty namespaces afterwards. Retrofitting Workload Identity in particular means recreating node pools — a maintenance window per cluster, which means the work never quite gets scheduled.

In plain terms: Take the application and package it into a container image. The decisions in this one file determine whether it survives contact with Kubernetes — most images that crash in production do so because of a choice made here, weeks before anyone noticed.

Most images that fail in production fail for the same handful of reasons. They run as root. They ignore the container memory limit. They do not handle SIGTERM, the signal Kubernetes sends to ask a process to shut down. And they ship an entire operating system worth of known vulnerabilities, catalogued as CVEs — Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures.

None is exotic, and all are fixed in the build rather than at runtime. The production pattern is a multi-stage build: one stage compiles the application with the full toolchain available, a second copies only the resulting artifact onto a minimal runtime base, creates a dedicated non-root user with a numeric ID, takes ownership of the application directory, drops to that user, and starts the process container-aware.
Shipping the build toolchain and source code to production. Cuts image size by 60–70% and removes a whole class of findings from vulnerability scan results
Rejection by Autopilot and hardened Standard clusters. Setting the user ID (UID) as a number rather than a username also lets the cluster validate that the container genuinely is not root

CrashLoopBackOff with exit code 137, the signature of an out-of-memory kill. Older Java Virtual Machines read the node's total memory rather than the container limit — on a 64 GB node with a 2 GB limit, the JVM sizes its heap for 64 GB and the kernel kills it
A Java Virtual Machine that has exhausted its heap but keeps its network socket open, failing health checks slowly while still accepting traffic

Test the image locally before it goes near a registry, and test it under constraint rather than on a laptop with 32 GB free — an explicit memory ceiling and a read-only root filesystem. The read-only filesystem is the important part: it surfaces every hidden write path at your desk, instead of at three in the morning when a pod reschedules.

Creating the repository and configuring Docker authentication against the regional host are one-time operations. After that the build, tag and push cycle is conventional — the only difference from older guides is the hostname, which now carries the region.

Once the image is pushed, retrieve its digest and deploy that, not the tag. Deploying by digest guarantees the image running in production is byte-identical to the one your pipeline tested. Mutable tags are how the wrong build reaches production without anyone changing a manifest.
Vulnerability scanning runs automatically on push, but the number it produces is only useful if something acts on it — a severity threshold wired into the pipeline as a build gate.

In plain terms: Create the environment the containers will run in. Several of these choices cannot be changed later without rebuilding the cluster or recreating every node pool, so they are worth getting right the first time.
Before any cluster operation will succeed, the Kubernetes Engine and Artifact Registry APIs need enabling on the project, and the default project and region set.

Autopilot creation is deliberately sparse: a name, a region, a release channel and a private-nodes decision, because Google manages the node layer. Standard creation is the opposite — a longer specification where the defaults are not the ones you want, and three choices are effectively permanent.
These are the ones worth slowing down for. Everything else on a Standard cluster can be adjusted after the fact; these three cannot, or not without work that will never be scheduled.
Without it, pods authenticate using node credentials or exported key files — the most common source of credential leaks in Kubernetes
Only by recreating every node pool
Pod and Service traffic use native VPC routes. The secondary IP ranges it derives are effectively permanent, and exhaustion cannot be fixed in place
A regional control plane spreads nodes across zones. Note that node count is specified per zone, so a three-zone region triples it — this surprises people at billing time

With Workload Identity enabled at the cluster level, the binding itself is a short sequence: create a Google service account, grant it only the roles the application genuinely needs, allow the Kubernetes service account to impersonate it, and annotate the Kubernetes service account so the cluster knows which identity to present.

The binding string is where this goes wrong. It names a project, a namespace and a Kubernetes service account, and a mismatch in any of the three produces the same symptom — the pod authenticates as the node's default service account instead.

Verify it explicitly rather than assuming. Run a throwaway pod in the target namespace using the service account in question and ask it which identity it holds. If the answer is the Compute Engine default service account, the binding did not take.
In plain terms: Tell the cluster how to run your container: how many copies, how to health-check them, how much memory they get, and how to replace them without dropping traffic.

A Deployment containing nothing but an image reference and a replica count will deploy successfully. It will also drop traffic on every rollout, every node upgrade and every preemption. The manifest that does not do this is not much longer, but it is deliberate about five things.
Memory limit equal to request, and no CPU limit

Memory is incompressible — exceeding the limit means the kernel kills the process, so matching request and limit earns the Guaranteed Quality of Service (QoS) class. A CPU limit instead causes throttling, which presents as unexplained latency while the node sits at 30% utilisation

A startup probe gives a slow legacy application time to boot without the liveness probe killing it mid-start. Using one probe for all three jobs is why legacy applications restart-loop on Kubernetes but ran fine on a VM
A pre-stop delay plus a generous termination grace period

Kubernetes removes the pod from the load balancer and sends SIGTERM at the same moment. Without the delay, the pod stops accepting connections before load balancers have finished draining, and clients see HTTP 502 errors
Capacity dipping below the replica count mid-deploy. A pod is added before one is removed, rather than the other way round
The scheduler legitimately placing all three replicas on one node, turning a single node failure into a full outage

Set the pod-level security context from the first deploy rather than as a hardening pass later: non-root numeric user, no privilege escalation, all Linux capabilities dropped, root filesystem read-only with a small writable volume for temporary files.

A PodDisruptionBudget sets a floor on how many replicas should remain available during voluntary disruptions such as node upgrades or autoscaler scale-down. Without an appropriate budget and sufficient replica distribution, maintenance activity may reduce application availability. The workload team remains responsible for defining and testing that availability policy.

After fetching cluster credentials and applying the manifests, watch the rollout to completion rather than trusting that it finished. Two checks are worth making immediately: confirm the pods landed in different zones, and compare live CPU and memory usage against the baseline captured from the legacy system.
The temporary fourth pod in Figure 10 is the setting working correctly: capacity goes up before it comes down, so there is no window in which the service runs below its replica count.

A Horizontal Pod Autoscaler adjusts replica count against observed CPU utilisation between a floor and a ceiling. The critical detail is that it computes utilisation as a percentage of the CPU request — so an autoscaler attached to a Deployment with no CPU request does nothing at all, silently, while appearing to be configured.
Set a stabilization window on scale-down as well. Without one, spiky traffic makes the workload oscillate every fifteen seconds.
In plain terms: Move real users from the old system to the new one a slice at a time — 5%, then 25%, then 50% — checking at each stage. If something looks wrong, you move the traffic back in seconds.

A single Domain Name System (DNS) cutover gives you one shot and a rollback that takes as long as the record's time to live (TTL). A weighted shift lets you move 5% of production traffic, watch what happens, and reverse it in seconds.

The mechanism is straightforward. Expose the legacy VM to the cluster as a Service with no selector — the absence of a selector is what stops Kubernetes managing the endpoints itself and lets you point them at a machine outside the cluster — and register the VM's internal address as an endpoint. From the cluster's perspective the legacy VM is now just another backend.

With both backends addressable, an HTTP Route splits traffic between them by weight. Promotion is then a matter of editing two integers: reduce the legacy weight, raise the new one, apply. Rollback is the same edit in reverse — in seconds, with no image rebuild, no DNS propagation and no deploy pipeline anywhere in the path.
Advance on evidence, not on a schedule. All four gates must hold for the full soak window at each stage before the next weight increase.
HTTP 5xx server-error rate on the new backend
Any elevation above the legacy baseline
p95 and p99 against the captured baseline
p99 above baseline for more than 5 minutes
Out-of-memory kills, CPU throttling, autoscaler behaviour
Any out-of-memory kill, or the autoscaler pinned at its maximum replica count

Soak through at least one full business cycle at 50%, including a peak-hour window and whatever your equivalent of month-end is. Migrations that look clean at three on a Tuesday afternoon routinely fail at nine on Monday morning.
In plain terms: Shut down the old system properly: stop it rather than delete it, take a snapshot first, and close off the credentials it was using.
Only after the soak window closes. The sequence is: confirm nothing still routes to the legacy backend, remove the legacy Service and its endpoints, snapshot the disks, and then stop the instance.

Stop the virtual machine before considering deletion. A short retention window gives the team time to identify undocumented dependencies, scheduled jobs, or validation gaps while preserving a reversible rollback option. The exact retention period should follow the organisation's change, backup, cost, and data-retention policies.
Deleting the disks is a separate decision, taken later, by someone with the authority to accept that it is irreversible.

Two checks close the loop. Confirm no user-managed service account keys remain — if the identity model was built correctly there will be none — and require signed images before admission, so only artifacts your pipeline produced and attested can run in the cluster.
Move Binary Authorization from dry-run to enforced mode once the pipeline produces attestations reliably.
These seven account for the overwhelming majority of post-migration incidents. Each has a specific diagnostic.
CrashLoopBackOff, exit code 137, no application error
The language runtime ignores the container memory limit and sizes its heap for the whole node
Set container-aware heap sizing for the runtime in use. Confirm by describing the pod and checking for an OOMKilled last state
Requests exceed any schedulable node, or the pod IP range is exhausted
Describing the pod shows which. IP exhaustion needs a new node pool with a different range — it cannot be fixed in place
The node service account lacks Artifact Registry read access, or the manifest still points at gcr.io
Grant the Artifact Registry Reader role on the repository, and repoint the image at the regional pkg.dev host
No readiness probe, or no pre-stop delay before SIGTERM
Add a readiness probe, a pre-stop delay, and a termination grace period long enough to cover it
Worked on the VM, permission denied in the container
The application ran as root on the VM; the container runs as a non-root user
Fix ownership at build time. Do not solve this by running as root
Cannot reach Cloud SQL or Cloud Storage from the pod
The Workload Identity annotation is missing, or the Identity and Access Management (IAM) binding names the wrong namespace and service account pair
Verify with the identity check from Step 2. The binding names a project, a namespace and a Kubernetes service account, and all three must match
The application writes to the container filesystem
Mount a PersistentVolume or externalize the state. A read-only root filesystem catches this in staging instead of production
A container filesystem is ephemeral. Any data required after a restart must use a PersistentVolume or an external data service.
Not every problem in this guide is a first-line fix. These are the ones to hand on rather than work around.
A symptom listed in the failure table above, with a matching diagnostic
Handle it. The fix is in the table and the diagnostic confirms the cause
Escalate. This cannot be fixed in place — it needs a new node pool on a different range, which is a design change
Choosing memory and CPU requests for a workload that has never run on GKE
Escalate. Requests should come from measured usage on the legacy system, not from a guess made under deadline
Advancing or halting a canary when the gates are ambiguous
Escalate. A clear gate failure means halt. Anything less clear is a judgement call that needs the service owner
Any change to IAM bindings, Workload Identity, or Binary Authorization policy
Escalate. These are security controls; changing them to unblock a deploy is how incidents start
Deleting the legacy virtual machine or its disks
Escalate. Stopping is reversible, deleting is not. This needs the service owner's sign-off
No. Workloads that require host access, kernel modules, specialised appliances, or unsupported licensing models may be better suited to Compute Engine or deferred until refactoring is practical.

Keep rollback available until the migrated service has passed the agreed validation and soak criteria, including representative peak periods. The duration should be defined by the service owner and aligned with change, backup, cost, and data-retention policies.

Start with state, storage paths, ports, external dependencies, identity, startup and shutdown behaviour, resource usage, operational ownership, and recovery requirements. The assessment should produce evidence, not only meeting notes.

Choose based on workload behaviour, operational control, governance, networking, cost allocation, and platform-management requirements. A mixed operating model may be appropriate where supported, but the decision should be validated against current Google Cloud documentation and organisational standards.
Use a staged traffic shift with measurable promotion gates for errors, latency, saturation, and data integrity. Test the rollback procedure before production traffic is moved.
The main migration challenge is identifying assumptions inherited from virtual machines, including unrestricted memory, persistent local disks, root access, and predictable shutdown behaviour.
Rescheduling, upgrades, memory pressure, and autoscaling expose these assumptions during normal platform operation.

Three habits make the difference. Work workload by workload rather than in waves, so that a discovery on one does not block forty. Size from measurement rather than from the old VM's specification sheet. And make the cutover a weighted shift with a rollback you have actually executed at least once, rather than one you are confident would work.
Applied together, these practices help teams detect issues during low-risk canary stages while the legacy rollback path remains available.
Intended Reader: Hands-on engineers and operators doing the migration work, not high-level approvers.
Prerequisites: Requires Linux, container, and cloud experience; no prior Kubernetes knowledge needed.
Platform & SRE: Cutover sequences, permanent settings, failure-mode diagnostics, and canary gates.
Architects & DevOps: Workload strategies, reference architectures, and supply chain security (digest deploys, image signing).
Reading Path: Beginners must read sequentially; GKE veterans should review the initial platform updates to unlearn outdated practices.
No Copy-Paste Scripts: Omits raw code commands so teams intentionally configure their own regions, IPs, and service accounts.

/newsroom/finding-sensitive-data-in-azur.title: Finding Sensitive Data in Azure Cloud Storage: Why Checking Files One by One Just Doesn’t Work
/newsroom/finding-sensitive-data-in-azur.description: In many organizations, cloud storage quietly fills up with reports, logs, exports, backups, and all kinds of files. Some of those files may contain PII, confidential records, or other sensitive information.
h1: The Problem with Checking Files Manually
The Solution: Microsoft Purview Data Map and Unified Catalog
Benefits of Microsoft Purview Data Map
Steps to Register and Scan Data from Azure Blob Storage
h2: Finding Sensitive Data in Azure Cloud Storage: Why Checking Files One by One Just Doesn’t Work
h6: Finding Sensitive Data in Azure Cloud Storage: Why Checking Files One by One Just Doesn’t Work
p: Finding Sensitive Data in Azure Cloud Storage: Why Checking Files One by One Just Doesn’t Work

In many organizations, cloud storage quietly fills up with reports, logs, exports, backups, and all kinds of files. Some of those files may contain PII, confidential records, or other sensitive information.
Have you ever stopped to think about what is sitting inside your Azure Cloud Storage?

Now imagine trying to open and review thousands—or even 1 lakh files—just to find out which ones contain sensitive data. That is not just time-consuming; it is almost impossible to do reliably. This is where a smarter way to discover and protect sensitive data becomes important.

Cloud storage grows faster than most teams realize. Every day, people upload documents, logs, images, backups, and application files. Before long, the storage account becomes a huge collection of data that keeps changing.

If you only have a handful of files, manual review might be fine. But when there are thousands of files, it quickly becomes slow, inconsistent, and easy to get wrong. One missed file with personal information, financial data, credentials, or confidential business records can create a real security or compliance risk.

That is why automated sensitive data discovery matters. Instead of checking each file one by one, security teams can use cloud security tools to scan storage accounts, detect sensitive information, and focus first on the areas that need attention.

This is where Microsoft Purview Data Map and Unified Catalog can make the process much easier. Instead of depending on manual checks, Microsoft Purview helps you build a clear view of your data estate by scanning data sources, capturing metadata, and making those assets easier to find and understand.

With Data Map, you can connect to supported data sources and scan them to collect technical metadata such as file names, schemas, columns, and classifications. This gives security and governance teams a better starting point than opening files one by one.

Once the data is scanned and ingested, Unified Catalog provides a searchable experience where teams can discover data assets, understand what they contain, and use governance metadata such as classifications, glossary terms, and data quality information to make better decisions.

In simple terms, Purview helps turn a messy storage environment into something more visible, searchable, and manageable. You can identify where sensitive data may exist, assign ownership, improve governance, and focus your review efforts on the files and locations that matter most.

The biggest benefit of Microsoft Purview Data Map is visibility. It helps you move from guessing what is inside your storage account to knowing what data assets exist, where they are located, and what metadata is available for them.
Better data discovery: Data Map scans supported sources and captures metadata, so teams can find data assets faster without manually checking every file or folder.
Improved classification: Built-in scanning and classification help identify sensitive or important data, making it easier to focus on areas that need protection.
Centralized metadata: Technical, business, operational, and semantic metadata can be stored in one place, giving teams a more complete understanding of the data estate.
Always-updated inventory: Scans can be scheduled so the Data Map stays current as new files and assets are added over time.
Stronger governance: By adding ownership, glossary terms, descriptions, and relationships, organizations can make data easier to manage, trust, and use responsibly.

So instead of treating Azure Cloud Storage like a black box, Data Map gives you a structured and searchable foundation. It helps security, compliance, and data governance teams understand the data landscape and act with more confidence.
An Azure Account with Active Subscription
Entra ID Tenant. Your users and services rely on this for authentication and RBAC.
You will need to be a Data Source Admin and Data reader to register a source and manage it in the Purview.
Configure the authentication method in the azure blob storage to have access to scan. The below options are supported:

Managed Identity (Recommended) – As soon as the Purview account is created, a system identity is created automatically in Azure AD tenant. Depending on the type of resource, Specific RBAC Role assignments are required for the Azure purview MSI to perform the scans.
Step 1: Enterprise Purview Account is Required to get Started with Data Map.
Navigate to Purview Portal Settings > Account > Upgrade Account
Link Azure Subscription and Resource Group
After Linking Purview Account is Automatically Created in the Azure portal
Step 1: Navigate to Microsoft Purview Data Map Solution Then Navigate to Domains then Create a New Collection.
A Domain is the highest level of organization in the Purview Data Map. It represents a major business unit, subsidiary, or environment and provides logical isolation for governance resources.
A Collection is a child of a Domain and is used to organize data sources, scans, and assets. Collections mainly provide operational organization and access control.
Step 2: Complete the Details for the Collection and Define the Collection Admin.
A Collection Admin is a user who manages a specific collection in Microsoft Purview by administering its data sources, scans, assets, and access permissions within that collection.
Step 3: Navigate to Data Source and Click on Register.s
Step 4: Select Azure Blob Storage from the Available Data Sources to Register then click on continue.
Step 5: Provide the Name for the Data Source and Map the Blob Storage you want to register from the Azure subscription then Map Under the Domain and Collection.
Once your Register the Data Source it will Appears under your Collection.

To establish secure authentication between the Azure Storage Account and Microsoft Purview Data Map, a credential must be configured. Microsoft Purview supports the following credential methods for Azure Blob Storage scanning:

Managed Identity enables Microsoft Purview to authenticate to Azure Blob Storage using Microsoft Entra ID without storing secrets or credentials. Access is controlled through Azure RBAC by assigning the required roles to the managed identity.

Account Key authentication allows Microsoft Purview to connect to Azure Blob Storage using the storage account access key. The key is securely stored as a credential in Purview and used during scan execution

It enables Microsoft Purview to authenticate to Azure Blob Storage using a Microsoft Entra ID application. Authentication is performed using the Tenant ID, Application (Client) ID, and Client Secret, while access is controlled through Azure RBAC by assigning the required roles to the Service Principal.
Managed Identity (Recommended), Service Principal, Account Key
Choose the authentication method based on your network environment. In this blog, we will use Managed Identity as the preferred authentication method.
Step 1: To Establish Connection Between Blob Storage and Purview Account Navigate to your storage account then Navigate to Access Control.
Step 2: Click on Add then Add Role Assignment Then Select Storage Blob Data Reader role.
Step 3: On the Members tab Select Managed Identify then assign to your Azure Purview Account Then Save.
Step 4: To validate the Authentication and Role access Navigate to your Data Source Page then click on new Scan.
Step 5: To validate the Authentication, Click on the Test Connection and Confirm the Same.
After the registration and authentication are successfully configured, we can begin scanning and classifying the data stored in Azure Blob Storage.
Step 1: Setup the Scan Configuration page name Your Scan then Configure the Managed Identify Credential for the Scan.

p: As the customer expanded globally, its AWS infrastructure became the backbone for AI-driven analytics, clinical data management and secure collaboration with healthcare authorities. However, rapid growth brought challenges in maintaining governance, backup compliance and operational visibility in their AWS environment.

The customer's AWS footprint had grown organically over several years, resulting in inconsistent security configurations across accounts and regions. Prior point-in-time audits had flagged issues but left the organization without a consolidated, risk-ranked view of its true exposure. With sensitive research and healthcare-adjacent data in scope, the stakes for getting this right were high, and the customer needed a partner who could assess the full estate without disrupting live workloads.

Quadra's security team conducted a full AWS Well-Architected Framework Review across all five regions, combining automated posture scanning with manual validation of high-risk areas. The assessment covered IAM configurations, network exposure, data protection controls, logging and monitoring coverage, and encryption practices across the customer's entire multi-account environment. Every finding more than 14,000 in total  was catalogued, severity-ranked, and mapped back to specific AWS accounts, services, and business risk.

Rather than handing over a static report, Quadra's team translated the findings into a structured remediation roadmap, built around Service Control Policies (SCPs) and Resource Control Policies (RCPs) to enforce guardrails at the organization level, alongside account-specific fixes for the highest-severity issues. The roadmap was delivered as both a prioritized tracker and an executive-level PowerPoint summary, giving the customer's leadership and engineering teams a shared view of what needed to happen and in what order.

The customer moved from a fragmented, undocumented security posture to a fully catalogued risk inventory with a clear, phased path to remediation. Org-wide guardrails closed entire categories of risk in a single implementation step rather than requiring per-account fixes, and the customer's compliance and security teams gained a shared, defensible record of their posture ready to support their next audit cycle and ongoing risk conversations with leadership.

Every prior audit finding was remediated and tracked to closure ahead of the customer's compliance deadline. h5: It Means You Get a Visionary Partner
It Means You Get Proven Adaptability
It Means You Get a Blueprint Built on Trust
p: For 25 years, our journey has been defined by one core principle: looking beyond the immediate horizon to architect what's next. Our annual calendars have served as a public record of our evolving perspective—a year-by-year chronicle of our commitment to guiding our partners through every major technology shift, from the dawn of the cloud to the era of AI.

Since our early days, we have used our annual calendar as more than just a marketing tool. It has been our public thesis—a declaration of the strategic themes we believe will define the coming year and a compass to guide our partners' thinking.

This visual history is the ultimate proof of our enduring philosophy. It shows that we don't just react to change; we anticipate it. We don't just follow trends; we help our partners architect a strategic response to them. From championing virtualization during the financial crisis to advocating for a data-first approach long before it was mainstream, this timeline demonstrates our long-term commitment to your long-term success.
Explore our journey below and see the evolution of the ideas that have shaped our industry and the blueprints we've used to architect our partners' ambition.

From our earliest days, we understood that true partnership required proving our capabilities on a global stage. This award marked the beginning of a relentless pursuit of excellence, setting a standard that would become the bedrock of our customer trust for decades to come.

In the midst of the Global Financial Crisis, when many viewed technology as a cost to be cut, we championed a contrarian view. Our guidance to partners was that smart, strategic IT was not a luxury, but a critical lever for survival and efficiency. Our focus shifted to architecting solutions—like virtualization and process optimization—that enabled businesses to do more with less, navigate the downturn, and emerge stronger and more resilient.

We posited that sustainable IT was not merely an environmental responsibility but a powerful driver for business efficiency. We advised partners that "Green IT" was a direct path to reducing operational costs and optimizing resources.

As the new decade began, we identified cloud computing, virtualization, and mobile applications as the game-changing, disruptive forces that would redefine enterprise IT, urging our partners to architect their strategies around this new reality.

We urged leaders to shift their thinking about cloud from a product to a fundamental utility, as impactful as electricity. The key question was no longer if cloud, but how to architect a business strategy around this new consumption model.

We formally stated that customer-centricity was not a process to be followed, but the core of our DNA. We argued that the ultimate measure of any technology's success was the success and satisfaction of the customer who used it.

We declared that competitive advantage no longer came from simply adopting technology, but from strategically applying it to drive measurable business outcomes. The role of the CIO had to evolve from a service moderator to a strategic, transformational agent.

We evolved the cloud narrative, framing it as an "omnipresent fabric" that would seamlessly connect data and deliver intelligence across all devices. This concept moved beyond infrastructure to a vision of an interconnected world.

By this time, "digital" was no longer a future concept; it was a present-day reality. Our focus evolved from advocating for technology adoption to ensuring its business impact. We argued that the true "moment of truth" for any technology solution is when it delivers measurable value—growth, profitability, and a competitive edge. Our role was to serve as the strategic bridge, architecting the solutions that directly connected technological capabilities to business outcomes.

With the market saturated by cloud hype, we pivoted from evangelism to strategic counsel. We argued that success required aligning the right cloud model—public, private, or hybrid—to specific business and IT roadmaps, championing clarity over blind adoption.

As the technology landscape grew increasingly complex, we asserted that Quadra's primary value was not just implementation, but strategic guidance. We positioned ourselves as a "Technology GPS" to help our partners navigate complexity and find the clearest path forward.

We identified AI as the driving force of the next industrial revolution. Our message was proactive: leaders should not just prepare for this shift, but partner with us to actively architect their company's role in creating this new future.

We championed a sophisticated evolution of customer-centricity: true partnership means starting with the customer's unique business need and then architecting the ideal solution, rather than pushing pre-defined products.

Marking our 20th year, we defined our most valuable asset: our culture. We stated that our longevity and success were a direct result of a deeply ingrained culture of customer obsession, which serves as our brand's ultimate promise.
